ai.definition: Recursive Neural Networks (RNNs) are a class of artificial neural networks designed to analyze structured data like trees or graphs by recursively processing their elements in a hierarchical manner.
ai.howItWorks: RNNs process input sequences by breaking them down into smaller, more manageable parts and then reassembling the output. They maintain a memory state that captures information from previous steps, allowing them to handle complex relationships within data structures.
ai.problemSolved: Handling and understanding hierarchical or nested data in tasks such as natural language processing (NLP) and graph analysis where linear models are insufficient.
ai.manufacturing: Not applicable. RNNs are software-based models designed and trained using programming languages like Python, frameworks like TensorFlow or PyTorch, and datasets relevant to the task at hand.
ai.buildProcess: Designing the network architecture, preparing training data, training the model on a GPU cluster, fine-tuning parameters, and validating performance against test data.
ai.costDrivers: Computational resources (GPU/CPU), time for training, expertise in deep learning, and quality of the dataset used for training.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Continuing development with potential commercialization as applications expand.
ai.regulation: Varies by application; NLP models may face data privacy concerns under regulations like GDPR or CCPA, while graph analysis might be subject to industry-specific compliance requirements.
ai.risks: Overfitting, model bias, and computational inefficiency during training are common risks. Ensuring ethical use of AI is also a critical concern.
ai.profitability: Potential for high profitability in industries where NLP or graph analysis can significantly enhance operations, but requires robust validation and adoption strategies.
ai.futureDevelopment: Improvements in efficiency, interpretability, and scalability to handle larger datasets and more complex structures are expected.

glossary.def: A type of deep learning model designed to process hierarchical or nested data.
Data structured in a tree-like form, where elements are organized into parent-child relationships.
The field of AI that focuses on the interaction between computers and human language.
The process of extracting information from graph structures, such as social networks or molecular structures.

subsystems.name: Tree input representation
subsystems.role: recursive nets need a hierarchy, not a flat sequence, so each input is first cast as a tree.

subsystems.name: Leaf encoder
subsystems.role: turns the smallest units into vectors the composition function can combine.
parts: sub-token features where words are rare

subsystems.name: Composition cell
subsystems.role: the core operator: merges two child vectors into a parent vector, and is reused at every node.
parts: weight matrix (or tensor for multiplicative interaction)

subsystems.name: Gating and stability layer
subsystems.role: controls how much each child contributes so gradients survive deep trees.
parts: forget/input gates (as in a tree-structured LSTM)

subsystems.name: Training machinery
subsystems.role: learns shared parameters by walking the tree in both directions.
parts: loss over node or root labels

subsystems.name: Readout
subsystems.role: turns node vectors into answers — a class, a score or a generated structure.

buildSteps.title: Parse the data into trees
buildSteps.detail: Run a statistical or neural parser over text (or a compiler front end over code) to produce a binary or n-ary tree for every example.

buildSteps.title: Vectorise the leaves
buildSteps.detail: Replace each token with a pre-trained embedding; keep the tree topology in a stack or adjacency record so the recursion knows which pairs combine.

buildSteps.title: Define the composition function
buildSteps.detail: Choose an operator such as a shared weight matrix applied to the concatenated children, or a higher-order tensor if multiplicative interactions between children matter.

buildSteps.title: Forward recursion
buildSteps.detail: Walk the tree bottom-up: compose every sibling pair, then their parent, until the root holds one vector for the whole structure.

buildSteps.title: Backward pass through structure
buildSteps.detail: Run reverse-mode differentiation over the tree, accumulating gradients into the single shared parameter set at every node.

buildSteps.title: Add supervision at every node
buildSteps.detail: Label intermediate phrases, not just the root, so shallow nodes receive gradient and the shared weights learn useful compositions.

buildSteps.title: Stabilise for depth
buildSteps.detail: Introduce gates, normalisation and gradient clipping; test on trees deeper than those seen in training to expose vanishing gradients.

buildSteps.title: Evaluate and deploy
buildSteps.detail: Measure accuracy against sequence-based baselines, then batch and prune the tree computation for inference cost.

prerequisites.why: the architecture has no way to learn a hierarchy from raw text in its classic form — the tree must be supplied.
leaves need meaningful vectors before composition can build phrase meaning.
gradients must flow through a variable-shape recursion, not a fixed sequence of layers.
phrase-level sentiment treebanks exist for English, but equivalents for most languages, code and scientific text are scarce.
many small irregular operations per example make naive implementations slow without batched tree kernels.

pathway.milestone: sequence and attention models dominate text, while recursive cells survive in niche structured tasks
pathway.unlocks: a cheap inductive bias for source-code ASTs, chemical structures and formula parsing.

pathway.milestone: hybrids that bolt an explicit recursion onto a pre-trained transformer backbone
pathway.unlocks: better systematic generalisation — handling novel combinations of known parts.

pathway.milestone: standard benchmarks for compositional generalisation with tree-shaped supervision
pathway.unlocks: evidence on exactly when hierarchy beats raw sequence order.

pathway.milestone: recursive modules inside program-synthesis and planning systems
pathway.unlocks: models that produce and verify nested structures, such as code or proofs, natively.
